gap: No result ChatGPT got states that BLUETTI's own AC180 page and manual cap AC output at 1,500 W when the air is 30–40 °C (86–104 °F). On a summer market afternoon, that cap is the whole rating of a 1,500 W blender, so the blender and the running fridge can't share the AC180.
standout_why: I compared against these pages. portableenergylab.com, the cited rival, names no products and gives no model-specific compatibility or temperature limits. Our own Dealectric page, also cited, lists the AC180 as '1,800 W: yes' for a 1,500 W blender with no heat condition. voltandvalley.com covers the Elite 200 V2 expansion-pack exclusions and says its 3,900 W power lifting is for resistive loads only, but it doesn't list the AC180 or any heat derating. briconline.org gives no operating temperatures or derating; its only heat note is about one unit's runtime on a 95 °F day. bluettipower.com's AC70 page (ChatGPT's plain chat) wasn't about this. ChatGPT said only 'choose the Elite 200 V2 if temperatures are high' and gave no number.
decides: This changes the pick for warm-season markets. Above 86 °F the AC180's AC limit drops from 1,800 W to 1,500 W, so a 1,500 W blender alone uses the whole limit, and the fridge (plus anything else on AC) pushes it over. That leaves no headroom; it's not a thin margin. In summer the AC180 is only safe with a blender rated well under 1,500 W (about 1,300 W or less, leaving room for the fridge), or with the fridge unplugged while blending. Otherwise the Elite 200 V2 (2,600 W) is the pick, though I couldn't find its own heat limit. The AC180's battery can be extended with a B230/B300 through a P090D-to-DC7909 cable ($89). That adds stored energy for the day but adds no inverter power, so it doesn't fix the blender problem.

findings.label: AC output cap at 30–40 °C ambient
findings.source_title: BLUETTI AC180 Portable Power Station | 1800W 1152Wh - BLUETTI US
findings.note: Spec line reads 'Operating Temperature: 0°C–40°C (30°C–40°C: @1500W Max.)'. The page text came through with garbled degree symbols. The manualslib copy of the AC180 manual (manualslib.com/manual/3073286, p.12) gives the same thing in °F: 'Discharging: -4°F~104°F (86°F~104°F: @1500W Max.)'. Arithmetic: a 1,500 W blender alone hits the cap, so with the fridge also running, the combined load goes over 1,500 W.

findings.label: Rated AC output, surge, outlets, power lifting
findings.value: 1,800 W continuous across 4 × 120 V/15 A outlets; 2,700 W power lifting (the page names resistive heaters: hair dryers, kettles, heaters)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI AC180 Portable Power Station | 1800W 1152Wh - BLUETTI US
findings.note: Power lifting doesn't apply to a blender motor, so the motor-load ceiling is 1,800 W, or 1,500 W above 30 °C.

findings.label: Expansion battery route
findings.value: B80 (806 Wh), B230 (2,048 Wh) or B300 (3,072 Wh), up to 4,224 Wh total; B230/B300 connect with the P090D-to-DC7909 External Battery Connection Cable, $89
findings.source_title: External Battery Connection Cable - BLUETTI US
findings.note: The cable listing says 'P090D To DC7909 Applicable Models: EB150/EB240/AC180, Length: 59in/150cm'. The 4,224 Wh figure (1,152 + 3,072) is from bluettipower.com/pages/ac180. The AC180's DC input limit is 500 W (manual p.11: 'up to 1440W AC input and 500W DC input'; product page: 'Solar Input: 500W Max., VOC 12-60VDC, 10A'). So an attached pack is limited to the DC input rate (500 W at most) and adds no inverter power. The price came from the store's JSON.
